questions.q: What distinguishes a data-quality exception from a reconciliation exception?
options: There is no real difference between the two
Reconciliation exceptions can only be found with UNION ALL
Data-quality exceptions only apply to Receivables, never Payables
A data-quality exception looks wrong on its own, with no second table needed to detect it; a reconciliation exception is a mismatch between two numbers that should agree
questions.explain: A negative invoice amount is wrong by itself; an invoice-vs-paid mismatch requires comparing two sources to detect.

questions.q: Why would `WHERE invoice_amount <= 0` be a useful data-quality check on AP_INVOICES_ALL?
options: Because a normal invoice amount should be positive, so zero or negative values (outside intentional credit memos) often signal a data entry error
Because all invoices should have a negative amount
Because Oracle automatically rejects any invoice with a negative amount
Because invoice_amount is never populated for real invoices
questions.explain: Normal invoices should have positive amounts; unexpected zero/negative values are a common sign of bad data entry or incomplete imports.

questions.q: In the overpayment check, why does HAVING use `SUM(ip.amount) > i.invoice_amount` instead of `<> 0`?
options: There is no difference — both produce identical results
Because only the overpayment direction (paid more than invoiced) is being flagged here, which is operationally more urgent than underpayment
Because `<> 0` is invalid syntax in a HAVING clause
Because `>` always runs faster than `<>`
questions.explain: The check specifically targets one direction of discrepancy — paying more than was invoiced — rather than any mismatch in either direction.

questions.q: What does combining multiple exception checks with UNION ALL, each labeled with its own 'exception_type' column, accomplish?
options: It removes duplicate exceptions automatically
It converts all exceptions into reconciliation checks
It merges several independent exception-detection queries into a single labeled report
It is required syntax — exception checks cannot run separately
questions.explain: UNION ALL lets you stack several independently-defined checks into one combined result, with a label column identifying which rule flagged each row.

questions.q: Why is UNION ALL preferred over UNION when combining several distinct exception checks like this?
options: Because each check targets a different condition, so duplicate rows across checks are unlikely or irrelevant, and UNION ALL avoids the unnecessary deduplication cost
Because UNION cannot be used with a literal label column like 'Overpaid'
Because UNION ALL automatically adds the exception_type column
There is no reason — UNION would produce an error here
questions.explain: Since each check's condition is independent and a given invoice is unlikely to appear identically in two checks, UNION ALL's lack of deduplication is appropriate and faster.
